slides.title: Hyperbolic Geometry As A Measurement System
slides.notes: Open by framing the lecture as a shift in measurement, not a shift in drawing skill. The disk is familiar Euclidean paper, but its ruler changes as points approach the boundary. That one decision explains why the boundary is infinitely far away, why geodesics bend in the drawing, and why hyperbolic triangles have area measured by angle defect.

slides.title: What The Chapter Builds
slides.notes: Use this agenda to connect the chapter to the course arc. Chapter 3 supplied clines and Mobius transformations, Chapter 4 supplied the Erlangen viewpoint, and this chapter turns those tools into a working geometry. Emphasize that each model is a coordinate system for the same hyperbolic plane, so formulas should be checked by invariance.

slides.title: The Disk Boundary Is Infinity
slides.notes: Spend time on the metric density before discussing any curved lines. Students often think the boundary circle is an edge of the space, but it is not included. The diagram makes the key claim visual: equal-looking Euclidean steps near the boundary represent much larger hyperbolic travel than equal-looking steps near the center.

slides.title: Geodesics Meet The Boundary Orthogonally
slides.notes: Now turn the metric rule into straightness. In the Poincare disk, hyperbolic lines are Euclidean diameters or circular arcs that strike the boundary at right angles. The visual test is deliberately local: at each ideal endpoint, the geodesic circle must be perpendicular to the unit circle, not merely aesthetically curved.

slides.title: Mobius Maps Are Hyperbolic Motions
slides.notes: Link this slide back to inversions and clines. Disk-preserving Mobius transformations move points and geodesics while preserving the hyperbolic metric. The formula is less important than the behavior: one can recenter a calculation at the origin, compute there, and map the answer back without changing hyperbolic length or angle.

slides.title: The Half-Plane Is The Same Plane
slides.notes: Use the Cayley transform as a change of coordinates. The disk and upper half-plane pictures look different, but they encode the same geometry. Diameters and orthogonal arcs in the disk become vertical rays or semicircles orthogonal to the real axis in the half-plane, which is often more convenient for algebraic distance calculations.

slides.title: Distance Is A Cross-Ratio Computation
slides.notes: Introduce the distance formula as an invariant, not as a mysterious analytic expression. The two ideal endpoints on the same geodesic provide the reference scale. The logarithm of a cross-ratio records how far two interior points sit between those endpoints, and Mobius invariance explains why the answer is independent of the model.

slides.title: Circles Look Distorted Near Infinity
slides.notes: Use the notebook artifact to separate hyperbolic radius from Euclidean radius. A hyperbolic circle centered near the origin can look fairly round in ordinary coordinates, while one near the boundary is compressed toward the interior. The object is still metrically round; the distortion is caused by the model's nonuniform conversion from Euclidean to hyperbolic scale.

slides.title: Parallelism Splits Into Three Behaviors
slides.notes: This is the conceptual center of hyperbolic geometry. Through a point off a line, there are two limiting parallels that share an ideal endpoint with the given line, and many ultraparallels that do not meet it even at infinity. Ask students to identify the behavior by ideal endpoints rather than by Euclidean visual slope.

slides.title: Angles Survive, Lengths Do Not
slides.notes: The Poincare models are conformal, so Euclidean drawing angles equal hyperbolic angles at intersections. This is a gift for triangle work. Lengths and areas, however, are not Euclidean readings from the page. Keep pointing back to the metric density: angle measurement is local shape preservation, while length and area depend on the changing scale factor.

slides.title: Triangle Defect Is Area
slides.notes: State the theorem as a measurement principle. In curvature negative one, a hyperbolic triangle has angle sum less than pi, and the missing angle is exactly its area. This reverses Euclidean habit: large triangles do not have arbitrarily large angle sums; instead, their angles collapse as vertices move toward the ideal boundary.

slides.title: A Parameter Lab For Inspection
slides.notes: Treat the lab as a live diagnostic for the lecture. Moving triangle vertices changes Euclidean appearance, angle sum, and defect together. The instructor can ask students to predict which motion increases area, then check whether the computed defect responds consistently with the theorem and with the visual position of vertices.

slides.title: Common Mistakes To Catch
slides.notes: Use this warning slide before assigning computations. The most common errors are all model-confusion errors: treating the boundary as a reachable circle, using Euclidean length along arcs, calling every Euclidean circle arc a geodesic, or forgetting that the upper half-plane and disk pictures are related by a coordinate change.

slides.title: What To Carry Forward
slides.notes: Close by naming the durable tools. Hyperbolic geometry is the first place in the course where local measurement, transformation groups, ideal boundary behavior, and topology-facing intuition all meet. These ideas prepare the later chapters: elliptic geometry contrasts the boundary story, surfaces generalize curvature, and cosmic topology asks what global quotients of geometric spaces could model a universe.
